Statistics: program of study

The plan for the whole major, then every course with a link to its syllabus. Dates are estimates as of Oct 8, 2026. They move earlier as pretests let you skip lessons.

Overview

This major teaches mathematical statistics the way a good undergraduate program does, and then, if you choose, the first years of a graduate program. The main text is Casella and Berger's Statistical Inference (2nd edition), read from the first chapter to the last. You will write the proofs yourself. After that come four applied courses: regression, experiments and A/B testing, statistical computing, and Bayesian statistics.

Statistics meets four times a week. Each lesson takes two meetings: one to read about seven pages, one to work through the lesson and write a proof. Every chapter opens with a pretest. You have a math degree, so expect to skip a lot of the early probability.

What you'll be able to do

After Level I:

  • Design an A/B test, run it, and defend the result to a skeptical reader.
  • Read p-values and confidence intervals correctly and explain the usual mistakes.
  • Prove the main results of mathematical statistics: sufficiency, properties of maximum likelihood, the Neyman–Pearson lemma, interval construction, and large-sample theory.
  • Fit a regression or a generalized linear model, interpret it and say what's wrong with it.
  • Build and check a simple Bayesian model.

After Level II (optional):

  • Read a statistics or machine-learning theory paper and check its proofs.
  • Prove limit theorems with measure theory.
  • Use causal-inference methods: potential outcomes, causal graphs, weighting and matching.
  • Work at a first-year PhD level on estimation, testing, high-dimensional problems and adaptive experiments.

How the major is organized

Required courses (Level I). S201–S205 cover Chapters 1–5 (probability). S301–S304 cover Chapters 6–9 (inference). S401–S403 cover Chapters 10–12 (large-sample theory and regression). Then S310 applied regression, S320 experiments and A/B testing, S330 statistical computing, and S340 Bayesian statistics.

Optional courses. S190 history and philosophy of statistics, S195 measurement and ethics, three electives (S360 time series, S370 survey sampling, S380 statistical learning), S390 three real analyses from start to finish, S399 a capstone report, and S398 a closing conversation about what you read.

Level II is optional and only starts if you sign up for it: S500 analysis review, S501–S502 probability theory, S511–S513 estimation, testing and asymptotics, S520 linear model theory, S530 Bayesian data analysis, S540 causal inference, S550 high-dimensional statistics, electives S560–S580, S590 foundations seminar, S595–S596 a qualifying-exam-style check and a research project, and S598/S599 the closing conversation and thesis.

Pretests. Each chapter's pretest asks one concept question, one calculation and one proof for every section. A section you get fully right is skipped. Get the whole pretest right and the chapter closes after a one-page summary and the chapter check.

Order

Required courses run one at a time, in this order: S201 → S202 → S203 → S204 → S205 → S301 → S302 → S303 → S304 → S401 → S402 → S403 → S310 → S320 → S330 → S340. S330 only needs S205, so it can move earlier if you want a break from proofs. Optional courses fit in wherever you want them. S190 is light enough for a day you're tired.

The dates below assume no lessons get skipped. They're recalculated every time these pages are rebuilt, and pretests usually pull them earlier, especially in Chapters 1–4.

What it takes to finish

  • Level I: S201–S205, S301–S304, S401–S403, S310, S320, S330 and S340, each finished through lessons or by passing its pretest.
  • Level II: S500, S501, S502, S511, S512, S513, S520, S530, S540 and S550.

Books

In your library: Casella and Berger, and its solutions manual (only for checking your work); Bruce, Bruce and Gedeck, Practical Statistics for Data Scientists; Hand, Statistics and Measurement (Very Short Introductions); Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting (2nd edition); Abbott, Understanding Analysis; Fremlin, Measure Theory; Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability; Jaynes, Probability Theory.

Free online, please download before spring 2028: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd edition; your copy is unreadable); Efron and Hastie, Computer Age Statistical Inference; Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd edition); Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting (3rd edition). For Level II: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples; Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If; Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning; Lattimore and Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms.

To buy, in the order you'll need them: Agresti, Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models (S310); Kohavi, Tang and Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (S320); Salsburg, The Lady Tasting Tea (S190, any time). For Level II: Lehmann and Casella; Lehmann and Romano; van der Vaart; Keener; Imbens and Rubin; Wainwright; Lohr; Wasserman; Mayo; Robert and Casella.
